items.title: [Real Estate 101 #4] Why Rents Can Fall in a City Everyone Is Moving To
items.body:
> Real estate markets obey supply and demand — but the supply can't move, can't be built quickly, and is never quite identical, so prices and rents routinely overshoot in both directions before settling.

## Today's Concept

In an intro economics course, markets clear neatly: price goes up, sellers supply more, buyers demand less, and the market lands on an equilibrium price. Real estate follows the same logic — it just breaks most of the assumptions that make the logic fast and clean.

**Four features that make property markets different**

1. **Immobility (locality).** You can't ship a vacant apartment from Cleveland to Phoenix. Because the good is fixed in place, there is no single "U.S. housing market" — there are thousands of local markets, and they can move in opposite directions in the same quarter. Even within one metro, a 15-minute difference in commute creates a different submarket.

2. **Heterogeneity.** No two properties are identical: lot, floor plan, condition, light, school zone, the neighbor's dog. That's why houses need appraisals while shares of stock don't. There is no single quoted "price" — only a range of negotiated outcomes around an estimated value.

3. **Supply is inelastic in the short run.** Land entitlement, permitting, financing, and construction take years. When demand jumps this spring, the units that answer it deliver in 2028. So the short-run supply curve is close to vertical: a demand surge lands almost entirely on price, not on quantity. And new construction is small relative to what already exists — U.S. completions add roughly 1% to the housing stock in a typical year. The existing stock, and whether its owners choose to list, dominates supply.

4. **Thin markets and high transaction costs.** At any moment a neighborhood may have a handful of buyers and a handful of sellers. Information is private and uneven. Commissions, closing costs, title, and transfer taxes commonly add up to several percent of the price. High friction means transactions are slow and prices are negotiated, not auctioned to a single clearing number.

**What moves each curve**

- *Demand shifters:* household formation and migration, local jobs and income, mortgage rates (buyers shop the monthly payment, not the sticker price), credit availability, expectations about future prices, and the rent-versus-own tradeoff.
- *Supply shifters:* construction and land costs, zoning and permitting, developer financing, the pipeline already under construction, and — often the biggest one in a given year — how willing existing owners are to sell.

**Equilibrium, and how we actually observe it**

```
Equilibrium: quantity demanded = quantity supplied, at the market price
```

We almost never see that point directly in real estate. Instead, practitioners read proxies for how far the market is from balance:

- **Months of supply** = current inventory ÷ the monthly pace of sales. By long-standing convention in U.S. residential brokerage, roughly 4–6 months is considered balanced; well below that is a seller's market, well above is a buyer's market.
- **Vacancy rate vs. natural vacancy rate** on the rental side. Some vacancy is healthy — tenants move, units get turned. Estimates of the "natural" rate for U.S. rentals are usually cited in the mid-single digits; persistently above it, landlords cut rent or offer concessions.
- **Days on market** and the **share of listings with price cuts** — fast, if noisy, temperature checks.

Because supply answers years late, these markets cycle rather than settle. High prices trigger building; the building arrives after demand has cooled; the glut pushes prices down; construction stops; the next shortage forms. Equilibrium in real estate is less a resting place than a line the market keeps crossing.

## In Everyday Life: Austin, Texas

Austin is the cleanest recent illustration in the country.

**2020–2022 — demand shock.** Remote work, tech relocations, and heavy in-migration hit a metro that could not add units in months. Asking rents jumped more than 20% in 2021 alone, and home prices ran up sharply. Nothing about the housing stock had changed — the demand curve shifted right into a near-vertical short-run supply curve, and the entire adjustment came out in price.

**2023–2025 — the supply answer arrives.** Developers had responded, and Austin ended up with one of the highest apartment-completion rates per capita of any large U.S. metro. Those units delivered *after* the in-migration wave slowed. Vacancy climbed, concessions came back ("two months free"), and asking rents fell roughly 5% year over year in 2024 — among the steepest declines of any big metro, in a city people were still moving to. Demand kept growing; delivered supply simply grew faster.

**Meanwhile, on the for-sale side.** A homeowner holding a 3% mortgage from 2021 does not want to list and re-borrow near 7%. That's the **lock-in effect**, and it kept resale inventory unusually tight nationwide even as buyer demand weakened. Note what it is: a leftward shift in the supply of existing homes caused by nothing on a builder's cost sheet. It's a reminder that in real estate, "supply" mostly means *the stock whose owners are willing to trade today*.

And a Cleveland renter felt none of this. Different local market, different curves.

## Three-Line Recap

1. Real estate obeys supply and demand, but immobility, heterogeneity, thin markets, and high transaction costs mean the adjustment is local, slow, and negotiated.
2. Short-run supply is nearly fixed, so demand shocks show up in price first and in quantity only years later — which is exactly what produces boom-and-glut cycles.
3. We infer equilibrium from proxies — months of supply, vacancy versus natural vacancy, days on market — because the market rarely sits still long enough to show it.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**1.** Why does a sudden demand surge in a metro area push prices up so sharply, instead of just increasing the number of homes sold?

   A. Demand for housing is perfectly elastic
   B. Short-run supply is highly inelastic because construction takes years
   C. Buyers and sellers have identical information
   D. Transaction costs in housing are near zero

**2.** True or False: In U.S. residential brokerage convention, roughly 4–6 months of supply is treated as a balanced market, with less than that favoring sellers.

**3.** An owner with a 3% mortgage declines to sell because a new loan would cost 7%. In supply-and-demand terms, this is best described as:

   A. A rightward shift in demand for existing homes
   B. A leftward shift in the supply of existing homes
   C. A movement along the supply curve
   D. An increase in the natural vacancy rate

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Immobility (locality)** — Property is fixed in place, so supply cannot relocate to where demand is; markets are inherently local.
- **Heterogeneity** — No two properties are identical, which is why value must be appraised rather than quoted.
- **Short-run supply inelasticity** — The near-vertical supply curve created by multi-year entitlement and construction lags.
- **Months of supply** — Inventory divided by the monthly sales pace; a standard gauge of how far a for-sale market is from balance.
- **Natural vacancy rate** — The healthy baseline share of rental units that are empty due to normal turnover; rents tend to fall when actual vacancy runs above it.

---

*Answers: **1 — B.** With supply effectively fixed for years, a rightward demand shift is absorbed almost entirely by price. **2 — True.** It's a convention, not a law of nature, but 4–6 months is the standard reference band; below it, buyers compete for scarce listings. **3 — B.** The lock-in effect withdraws willing sellers from the market, shifting the existing-home supply curve left — even though construction costs never changed.*

items.title: [DAC 2025] What If Designing a Chip Was Just Writing Code?
items.body:
> At the world's biggest chip-design conference, UCLA's Jason Cong argued that the next wave of custom silicon should be designed by people who only know how to write software — and showed the AI tooling that is starting to make that possible.

## What He Presented

On June 25, 2025, Jason Cong — Volgenau Chair for Engineering Excellence Professor at UCLA's Computer Science Department — delivered a keynote at the 62nd Design Automation Conference (DAC), the field's premier event for the software that designs chips. His title: **"Democratize Chip Design — with Deep Learning and Automated Code Transformation."**

The problem he set out is easy to state. Today, if you want a custom chip or accelerator tuned to your particular workload, you need a hardware engineer. There aren't many of them, they're expensive, and the work takes months. Meanwhile, there are tens of millions of software developers who know exactly what their code needs — and no practical way to turn that knowledge into silicon.

A partial bridge already exists. It's called **high-level synthesis (HLS)**: you write ordinary C or C++, and a tool generates a hardware design from it. The catch is that the tool only produces something *fast* if you annotate the code with the right hints — directives called **pragmas** that tell it which loops to unroll, which memories to split apart, where to pipeline. Choosing them well is a combinatorial search over billions of possibilities, and getting it wrong can cost you a 100× slowdown. In practice, that's still expert work.

Cong's keynote laid out a vision for removing the expert from that loop, drawing on work at UCLA done in collaboration with Prof. Yizhou Sun's machine learning group. Three ingredients:

- **Deep learning as a fast stand-in for the slow tool.** Actually synthesizing a design to see how it performs can take hours. So the group trains **graph neural networks** on the program's structure — represented as a graph of operations and data flow — to *predict* speed and chip-area cost in seconds. Their HARP model adds a hierarchical view of the program and, importantly, separates the representation of the code from the representation of the optimizations applied to it, which helps the model generalize to programs it has never seen.
- **Mathematical programming instead of trial and error.** Rather than guessing pragmas one at a time, the group's Sisyphus framework folds loop restructuring, pragma insertion, and tile-size selection into a *single* optimization problem and hands it to a solver. In their published evaluation, that produced a geometric-mean speedup of roughly 6× over their own earlier AutoDSE tool on the kernels tested.
- **Agentic AI that rewrites the code, not just the annotations.** This is the "automated code transformation" in the title. Large language models are used not merely to sprinkle hints on your code, but to restructure it into a shape that maps well onto hardware — then check the result and iterate.

The direction has a track record. An earlier UCLA system, AutoDSE, matched the performance of hand-tuned vendor library kernels while using about 26× fewer optimization pragmas — averaging less than one pragma per design.

One honest note on scope: a keynote is a vision talk, not a single result. Cong was surveying a research program and where it's headed, not announcing a finished product.

## Why It Matters

For decades, chips got faster on their own — you wrote code, waited eighteen months, and it ran quicker. That escalator has largely stopped. The remaining way to get big gains is **specialization**: build hardware shaped around one specific job, whether that's a recommendation model, a genome aligner, or a video codec.

The bottleneck is no longer whether specialized hardware works. It's that almost nobody can build it. Every custom accelerator competes for the same scarce pool of hardware engineers, so only workloads at enormous scale — the ones that justify a multi-year, multi-million-dollar design effort — ever get one.

If a competent software developer could get a working accelerator out of their existing code, that calculus changes. The set of problems worth building custom silicon for expands enormously, and it starts to include work done by small teams and academic labs, not just hyperscalers.

There's precedent for this kind of shift. Programmers once hand-wrote assembly language because compilers weren't good enough. Once they were, the number of people who could write useful software increased by orders of magnitude. Cong is proposing the same move one layer down — with the compiler's role now played partly by learned models.

It's worth being clear about what remains unsolved. Automatically generated designs still trail expert hand-tuning on some workloads. The learned predictors need training data, and generalizing to code unlike anything in the training set is an open research problem — which is why the group also builds benchmark suites to measure exactly that. This is a credible direction, not a solved one.

## Making It Simple

Think of writing software as writing a recipe. It assumes one cook, one kitchen, one dish at a time — and any competent cook can follow it.

Designing a chip is not writing a recipe. It's designing the **factory**: how many stations, what moves down the conveyor belt in what order, where ingredients get stored so nothing waits. Handing your recipe to a factory architect gets you a production line, but only after months of expensive back-and-forth.

High-level synthesis was the first attempt at automating that translation — but it only worked if you also handed over detailed notes on how to lay out the floor ("run these two steps in parallel, split this pantry into four"). Writing those notes required knowing how factories work.

What Cong is proposing is a system that reads your recipe, *understands* it well enough to predict how a given factory layout would perform, rewrites the recipe where a different sequence of steps would run better on an assembly line, and designs the floor plan itself. You keep writing recipes. Something else figures out the factory.

## Three-Line Recap

1. At DAC 2025, Jason Cong (UCLA) argued that custom chip design should be accessible to ordinary software developers, not just hardware engineers.
2. His approach combines graph neural networks that predict hardware performance in seconds, mathematical solvers that pick optimizations globally rather than by trial and error, and LLM agents that rewrite source code into hardware-friendly form.
3. If it works at scale, building a custom accelerator becomes something a small team can attempt — though generated designs still trail expert hand-tuning on some workloads.

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **High-Level Synthesis (HLS)** — A tool that takes ordinary software code (typically C/C++) and generates a hardware circuit design from it.
- **Pragma** — A hint added to source code telling the synthesis tool how to build the hardware; the right ones can mean the difference between a fast design and a useless one.
- **Design Space Exploration (DSE)** — The search for the best combination of those hardware design choices among billions of possible configurations.
- **Graph Neural Network (GNN)** — A neural network that learns from data shaped like a network of connected nodes — here, a program represented as a graph of operations and the data flowing between them.
- **FPGA** — A reprogrammable chip whose circuitry can be reconfigured after manufacturing, widely used to prototype and deploy custom accelerators without fabricating a new chip.

---

**Sources:** [UCLA CS announcement](https://www.cs.ucla.edu/professor-jason-cong-presents-keynote-on-democratize-chip-design-at-the-2025-design-automation-conference/) · [UCLA VAST Lab](https://vast.cs.ucla.edu/news/2025-06/prof-cong-delivered-keynote-dac%E2%80%992025) · [DAC 2025 program](https://62dac.conference-program.com/presenter/?uid=322343) · [Keynote video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a-Sp2WHmig4) · [AutoDSE (ACM TODAES)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3494534) · [Sisyphus (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.03058v1)

items.title: The CDC Spent Nearly a Year Without a Confirmed Director. A 51–44 Vote Just Ended That.
items.body:
On August 5, the Senate voted 51–44 to confirm Dr. Erica Schwartz as director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — closing out a vacancy that had stretched for close to a year at the agency responsible for tracking and responding to disease outbreaks in the United States.

She becomes the CDC's 22nd director and the first Black woman to hold the post.

Both halves of that sentence deserve attention, but so does the number attached to it. A seven-vote margin, along a mostly party-line split, is not how the top job at a scientific agency was historically filled. For most of the CDC's history, it wasn't filled by a Senate vote at all.

---

## What the Senate actually did

The vote itself was procedurally ordinary and politically anything but. Fifty-one senators voted yes, forty-four voted no, and the tally broke largely along party lines.

What makes the outcome notable is that, only weeks earlier, the nomination looked finished. Schwartz had a rough outing before the committee that handles health nominations — the kind of hearing where a nominee absorbs sustained questioning, gives answers that satisfy few people in the room, and leaves with the whip count moving in the wrong direction. Nominations that stumble at that stage frequently do not recover. Senators quietly signal that they'd rather not have to vote, the White House quietly looks elsewhere, and the nomination expires without a floor vote ever being scheduled.

That is roughly what had already happened once in this seat. This time it didn't.

## Why the chair sat empty so long

The vacancy traces back to the summer of 2025.

The CDC director became a Senate-confirmed position beginning in January 2025, the result of a change Congress wrote into appropriations law in 2022. Before that, the director was appointed directly by the Secretary of Health and Human Services — no hearing, no floor vote, no confirmation fight. A president could install a new director in an afternoon.

The first director confirmed under the new rules took office in July 2025 and departed roughly a month later amid a public dispute over the agency's direction. Several senior CDC officials resigned in the days that followed. The agency was then run on an acting basis by an official detailed from the department's leadership — a workable arrangement for weeks, an awkward one for months.

A subsequent attempt to fill the job permanently did not survive the confirmation process. Meanwhile the agency absorbed budget reductions and staff departures that thinned out parts of its workforce.

The result was an institution operating for the better part of a year without a leader who could credibly say they'd be there in six months. That matters more than it sounds. Acting directors can keep the lights on, sign what needs signing, and manage an emergency if one arrives. What they generally cannot do is make multi-year commitments — reorganize divisions, launch long-horizon surveillance programs, or recruit senior scientists who want to know who their boss will be. Career staff learn to wait out temporary leadership. Vacancies at the top tend to freeze decisions several layers down.

## The office became partisan before the person did

It's tempting to read a 51–44 margin as a verdict on one nominee. It's more useful to read it as a verdict on the job.

Confirmation votes for public health agency leadership were not always contested affairs. The change in 2022 that made the CDC director subject to Senate confirmation was framed at the time as an accountability measure — a response to the sense, held in different forms across the political spectrum, that the agency had made consequential decisions during the pandemic without enough external check.

The predictable second-order effect is now visible. Once a post requires 51 votes, it acquires the properties of every other job that requires 51 votes. Nominees are evaluated partly on credentials and partly on which coalition they're understood to belong to. Hearings become opportunities to litigate the last five years of health policy with a person who wasn't in charge for any of it. And the seat can sit empty for a year, because an empty seat is a survivable outcome for everyone except the agency.

Accountability and paralysis turn out to be produced by the same mechanism. That's not an argument that the 2022 change was wrong — reasonable people land in different places on whether a director of a 10,000-person agency with emergency authorities should face a public vote. But it is the trade-off, and this vacancy is the clearest demonstration of it so far.

## What lands on her desk

The incoming director inherits a specific and unglamorous list.

**Staffing.** Budget reductions and resignations have left gaps, including in senior scientific ranks. Rebuilding takes longer than cutting, and the people who left had institutional knowledge that doesn't come back with the job posting.

**The advisory apparatus.** The CDC relies on outside expert committees whose composition and processes have been the subject of sustained public argument. How the new director handles those bodies will be an early signal of how much independence the agency's scientific process is understood to have.

**Trust, which is not one number.** Public confidence in the CDC is not uniformly high or uniformly low — it varies enormously by political affiliation, and the gap between groups is now wider than it was before 2020. A director cannot close that gap by communicating more clearly, though communicating clearly helps. It's a structural problem the agency did not create alone and cannot solve alone.

**The next outbreak, whenever it is.** This is the part no one can schedule. The practical test of any CDC director is how the agency performs in the first ninety days of something nobody saw coming — and that test is graded on preparation done long beforehand.

**Being the first.** The historic dimension of the appointment carries its own weight. Firsts are scrutinized differently, and the scrutiny doesn't lift after the first year.

## What we know, and what we don't

Worth separating clearly, because early coverage of any confirmation blends the two.

**Established:** the date, the 51–44 margin, the roughly party-line split, the length of the vacancy, and the historic nature of the appointment.

**Not yet established:** what she will actually do. Confirmation hearings are a poor predictor of governance. Nominees answer hypotheticals under adversarial conditions; directors make decisions under real ones with information the hearing room didn't have. Personnel choices in the first sixty days will say more than anything said in testimony.

**Contested:** essentially all of the surrounding interpretation. Whether the last year represents necessary correction or damaging disruption is a live political argument, and coverage of this confirmation will reflect whichever answer the outlet already holds. Reading across sources is more useful here than usual.

## Why this is worth following

The CDC is an agency most Americans think about only when something has gone wrong — which means the periods when nothing is going wrong are exactly when its capacity gets built or quietly eroded.

A confirmed director doesn't fix an agency. It restores the precondition for fixing one: someone with the standing to make decisions that outlast the news cycle, and the accountability that comes with having been voted on in public.

Whether the vote that ended the vacancy also ended the underlying instability is a separate question. Nothing about a 51–44 margin suggests the argument is over. It suggests the argument now has a permanent address.

---

*This article summarizes publicly reported developments as of August 7, 2026. Details of personnel decisions and agency policy may change; for official announcements, consult the CDC and the Department of Health and Human Services directly, and check current reporting from established news organizations for the latest developments.*

items.title: The Phones Went Dark First: Inside the Kashmir Protest Movement Pakistan Outlawed
items.body:
**A dispute over twelve legislative seats in Pakistan-administered Kashmir has become something larger: a stress test of how a state responds to a protest movement it cannot easily categorize. The connectivity blackout that accompanied the crackdown is also the reason nobody can say with confidence how many people have died.**

---

## The order of events matters

Most accounts of unrest begin with the unrest. This one begins with a signal drop.

On **June 5, 2026**, the government of Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) declared the Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee — the JAAC, the loose coalition that had organized the region's protest politics for three years — a proscribed organization under the **AJK Anti-Terrorism Act, 2014**. Internet access across the territory was curtailed the same day. The monitoring group NetBlocks confirmed a major disruption to connectivity, noting that the shutdown arrived *ahead* of the protests rather than in response to them, and was likely to limit coverage of what followed.

Two days later, on **June 7**, the AJK Supreme Court ruled that the twelve reserved assembly seats at the center of the dispute are constitutionally protected and cannot be abolished without a constitutional amendment — closing, at least judicially, the door the protesters had been pushing on.

The mobilization that had been building since talks collapsed in late May became a regionwide movement almost immediately. On **June 8**, initial clashes reportedly killed eleven people. On **June 9**, the JAAC called a general strike that shuttered markets, schools, and transport, concentrated most heavily in the **Poonch division**. By mid-June the reported toll had passed twenty.

The sequence — ban, blackout, court ruling, confrontation — is the story. It is also why the story is so hard to verify.

## What the twelve seats actually are

The AJK Legislative Assembly reserves twelve of its seats for **Kashmiri refugees who left Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir after the 1947 partition**, along with their descendants. Those voters live elsewhere in Pakistan — Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa — not in AJK.

To supporters of the arrangement, the seats are a constitutional and symbolic commitment: they keep the displaced population represented in the only Kashmiri assembly available to them, and they encode Pakistan's long-standing position that the Kashmir question is unresolved rather than settled by a border.

To the JAAC and its supporters, the seats are a governance problem with a very practical edge. Twelve seats in a 53-member house is not a rounding error. Because the electorate for those seats sits outside AJK, the argument goes, national parties headquartered in Islamabad and Lahore can assemble a bloc that does not answer to anyone who actually lives with AJK's electricity tariffs, wheat prices, road conditions, or hospital waiting rooms. The movement's complaint is not primarily about identity. It is about who holds the swing vote in a legislature that decides where money goes.

That distinction is what has made the movement difficult for the state to define. It is not separatist in the conventional sense, it is not aligned with a militant network, and its demands are budgetary and procedural rather than territorial.

## Thirty-eight points, not one

The seats have dominated coverage, but they are a single line in a **38-point charter of demands** the JAAC unveiled in September–October 2025 — itself an escalation of protest cycles running back to 2023 over electricity tariffs, flour subsidies, and everyday governance failures.

The charter is unglamorous by design. It asks for subsidized power and wheat, investigations into alleged corruption, better schools and hospitals, road and infrastructure spending, and reductions in official privileges and perks. It reads less like a manifesto than like a municipal audit.

Officials say most of it has already been delivered. Leaders in the governing Pakistan Peoples Party bloc have said **35 of the 38 demands** have been implemented, with the remainder blocked by cost, feasibility, or — in the case of the reserved seats — the courts. The JAAC disputes both the count and the quality of implementation. With independent verification constrained by the communications restrictions, that disagreement has no easy referee.

## Why the death toll is a range, not a number

This is the part of the story that resists a clean sentence.

- **Amnesty International**, on July 28, said at least **40 people** had been killed — 34 protesters and six police and paramilitary personnel.
- **Local residents and activists** have put the civilian figure higher, in the range of 50 to 60 or more.
- The **JAAC's own documentation** claims roughly 80 deaths.
- **Independent journalist Harris Qadeer** reported 89 deaths across Rawalakot and Mirpur by late July.
- The AJK and federal governments have **not published an official toll**.

Those numbers are not simply competing estimates from equally equipped counters. They are what happens when mobile networks and internet access in the affected districts are restricted for weeks, roadblocks limit movement, and reporters cannot reach the areas where the worst incidents are alleged to have occurred. NetBlocks documented severe restrictions from early June; connectivity monitors recorded limited service persisting into August.

A blackout does not just suppress information. It degrades it. In the absence of verifiable reporting, both inflated and deflated claims circulate freely, and the resulting fog becomes its own argument — for the state, evidence that the movement traffics in exaggeration; for the movement, evidence that the state is hiding something. Neither side can be checked, which is precisely the problem.

## What proscription does

Designation under the Anti-Terrorism Act is not a symbolic label. It converts organizing into a prosecutable offense, exposes bank accounts and property to freezing, and criminalizes participation, fundraising, and public advocacy.

Four JAAC spokespeople — **Shaukat Nawaz Mir, Sardar Umar Nazir, Khawaja Mehran Arshad, and Sardar Aman Khan** — were placed on wanted lists, with bounties reported at roughly $36,000 for information leading to arrests. Mir was arrested on June 30. Other organizers, including Syed Farhad Ali Shah in mid-June, were reported detained. On August 1, journalists **Razi Tahir and Muhammad Saif** were reported taken into custody in Islamabad.

**Amnesty International** called the terrorism designation of a protest movement "a dangerous escalation," and **UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk** joined calls for restraint and investigation into the use of force. India's foreign ministry also issued criticism — which Pakistan rejected as interference, with military spokesperson **Lieutenant-General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry** saying authorities had exercised "wisdom and restraint" and that the deployment of force remains solely a state prerogative.

The government's tone has not been uniform. AJK Prime Minister **Faisal Mumtaz Rathore** publicly offered dialogue. Federal Defence Minister **Khawaja Asif** took a markedly harder line, framing the protesters' obligation as obedience to the state. Both positions are official; they point in opposite directions.

## An election held in the dark

The crackdown collided with a scheduled local election, conducted in three phases:

| Phase | Date | Area |
|---|---|---|
| First | July 27 | Mirpur division |
| Second | August 2 | Muzaffarabad division |
| Third | August 10 (scheduled) | Poonch division |

The first phase coincided with a JAAC march and further deadly confrontations. Among those killed was **Sardar Usman Nazir**, brother of JAAC leader Sardar Umar Nazir. Nazir has denied that the movement is responsible for violence, alleging that incidents were staged — a claim the government rejects and which, like most claims in this dispute, cannot currently be independently assessed.

The JAAC called for a boycott. Authorities reported turnout above 50 percent and results favoring parties aligned with the federal ruling coalition in the early phases. The third phase is scheduled for **Poonch** — the division where the protests have been most intense and where verification has been hardest.

Whether a turnout figure means much under those conditions is a genuinely open question, and one that will be argued regardless of the final count.

## The actual test

Strip away the specifics and what remains is a problem states face more often than they admit: a movement with local, material, largely legalistic demands, no armed wing, and enough popular reach to shut down commerce across a territory.

Such a movement can be **negotiated with**, which concedes that grievances are legitimate and invites more of them. It can be **ignored**, which usually escalates. Or it can be **reclassified** — moved from the category of politics into the category of security, where a far wider set of tools becomes available and the question of whether the demands were reasonable stops being the operative one.

The June 5 proscription was that reclassification. It arrived *before* the mass mobilization, not after, and alongside a blackout that made the consequences difficult to document. That ordering is what critics point to, and it is the substance of the objection: not that the state acted, but that it defined the problem in a way that removed the need to answer it.

Whether that judgment holds up will depend on evidence that does not yet exist in verifiable form — accurate casualty records, an accounting of detentions, and reporting from Poonch. Restoring connectivity is the precondition for producing any of it.

---

## What to watch next

- **The August 10 Poonch phase** — the decisive test of whether the electoral process holds in the movement's stronghold.
- **Connectivity restoration** — the single best indicator of whether authorities expect further confrontation, and the gate on all independent verification.
- **The status of the proscription** — whether the ATA designation is maintained, narrowed, or challenged in court after the election cycle closes.
- **An official casualty accounting** — its release, or continued absence, will shape international pressure more than any statement.
- **The reserved seats question** — with the judicial route closed, the only remaining path is a constitutional amendment, which returns the issue to the legislature the protesters say is the problem.

---

### Editor's note on sourcing

Figures in this article are contested and attributed to their sources rather than presented as established fact. Communications restrictions in the affected districts have prevented independent verification of casualty counts, detention numbers, and specific incidents; reported totals from official bodies, rights organizations, journalists, and the movement itself differ substantially. This piece summarizes publicly reported information as of early August 2026 and takes no position on the underlying political dispute. Details may change as access improves.

### Sources

- [Pakistan-administered Kashmir elections and protests – all you need to know — Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/3/pakistan-administered-kashmir-elections-and-protests-all-you-need-to-know)

items.title: The Strongest El Niño in 70 Years Is Already Being Priced Into Next Year's Food Bill
items.body:
Weather shocks and grocery prices run on different clocks. The ocean warms this year; the shelf reprices next year. That gap — roughly twelve to eighteen months between a Pacific temperature anomaly and the number at the bottom of a receipt — is the single most important thing to understand about the El Niño now building in the equatorial Pacific.

Forecasters expect this event to rank among the strongest in at least seven decades. The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) has warned that if it develops as projected, it could push roughly **49 million additional people into acute hunger by the end of 2027**, layered on top of the **225 million already classified as food-insecure across 45 countries**. In response, the agency says it is committing about **$80 million to "anticipatory" relief** — money spent before a single harvest has failed.

That last detail is the story. Humanitarian agencies do not usually spend ahead of a disaster. When they do, it is a signal worth reading carefully.

---

## What El Niño actually does

El Niño is a periodic warming of surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific. The warm water shifts where the atmosphere's deepest convection sits, and that shift drags the global rainfall map with it. The pattern is not uniform, and it is not uniformly bad:

- **Drier than normal:** Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, eastern Australia, southern Africa, parts of Central America and northern South America, and often the Indian monsoon belt.
- **Wetter than normal:** the southern United States, the Horn of Africa, coastal Peru and Ecuador, parts of Argentina and southern Brazil.
- **Warmer than normal:** global mean temperatures typically spike in the year *following* the peak, because the ocean releases stored heat with a lag.

So a strong El Niño is not a global drought. It is a *reshuffling* — and the reshuffling happens to land hardest on regions that grow crops with narrow margins for error and hold few reserves.

---

## Why the damage arrives late

The intuitive model is wrong. Most people picture a storm, a ruined field, and empty shelves the following week. Agricultural systems do not fail that way.

Here is the actual sequence:

| Stage | Roughly when | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| Ocean warms, event peaks | Late 2026 – early 2027 | Rainfall patterns shift; little visible food impact |
| Planting season disrupted | Early–mid 2027 | Farmers plant late, plant less, or plant a different crop |
| Harvest comes in short | Mid–late 2027 | Yields fall; households eat their own stock rather than sell |
| **Lean season** | **Late 2027 – early 2028** | Stocks run out before the next harvest; prices spike locally |

The **lean season** is the interval between the exhaustion of one harvest's stores and the arrival of the next. In much of southern Africa it runs from roughly October to March. A household that harvested 40% less than usual does not feel it in July — it feels it in December, when the granary is empty and the market price has already climbed because everyone else's granary is empty too.

This is why the WFP's stated timeline points at **2027–28**, not 2026. The event is happening now. The consequence is scheduled.

---

## How it reaches a US grocery cart

American consumers are insulated from most of this — but not all of it. Three things are worth separating.

**1. The farm-gate share of retail price is small.** For a box of cereal or a loaf of bread, the raw grain is typically a low-single-digit to low-double-digit percentage of what you pay. Labor, packaging, transport, energy, and retail margin dominate. A 30% move in wheat futures does not become a 30% move at the register.

**2. Some categories are far more exposed than others.** The commodity share is much higher — and the growing regions much more El Niño-sensitive — for:

- **Coffee** (Brazil, Vietnam, Indonesia)
- **Cocoa** (West Africa, where rainfall timing matters enormously)
- **Palm and vegetable oils** (Indonesia and Malaysia, both classic El Niño dry-signal regions)
- **Rice** (India and Southeast Asia; also the category most prone to export restrictions)
- **Sugar** (India, Thailand, Brazil)
- **Spices, nuts, and tropical fruit**

These are the line items where a Pacific anomaly shows up most legibly in US retail.

**3. Policy amplifies more than weather does.** The sharpest food price moves of the past decade were rarely caused by a harvest shortfall alone. They were caused by a shortfall *plus* an export ban. When a major rice or wheat exporter restricts shipments to protect domestic supply, world prices can move more in a week than a bad monsoon moves them in a season. Watch trade policy at least as closely as rainfall.

A fourth, quieter channel: **logistics.** Reduced rainfall in the Panama Canal watershed has previously forced draft restrictions and transit auctions, raising freight costs on routes that have nothing to do with the affected crop. Shipping is a cost input to everything.

---

## Why spend $80 million before anything breaks

"Anticipatory action" is a relatively recent shift in humanitarian practice, and the logic is straightforward arithmetic.

Money spent *before* a shock buys different things than money spent after. Beforehand, it buys drought-tolerant seed, small-scale irrigation repair, veterinary support to keep livestock alive, cash transfers that let families avoid selling productive assets, and prepositioned grain in warehouses reachable before roads wash out. Afterward, it buys emergency airlifts and therapeutic feeding — the most expensive interventions in the catalogue, delivered at the point of maximum logistical difficulty.

Agencies working on early-warning-triggered financing have generally found the pre-positioned dollar goes considerably further than the post-crisis dollar, and there is a second effect that is harder to quantify: households that do not have to sell their oxen, their seed stock, or their roof to survive a lean season recover in one year instead of five. Distress asset sales are how a single bad harvest becomes a decade of poverty.

The constraint is not the analysis. It is that anticipatory funding requires donors to release money against a forecast — before there are pictures, and before the story is on any front page. That is a genuinely hard institutional ask, which is why $80 million is a notable number even though it is small against the scale of the projected need.

---

## What to actually watch over the next year

If you want to track whether this plays out as forecast, a handful of indicators carry most of the information:

- **ONI (Oceanic Niño Index) values** published by NOAA's Climate Prediction Center — the standard measure of event strength, and the one that determines whether "strongest in 70 years" holds up.
- **The Indian monsoon's June–September performance**, and whether India's rice export policy shifts in response.
- **FAO's monthly Food Price Index**, especially the vegetable oils and cereals sub-indices.
- **Southern African planting reports** from roughly November onward — the first hard evidence on 2027 output.
- **Any announced export restriction** from a top-five exporter of rice, wheat, or vegetable oil.

---

## The honest caveats

Seasonal forecasts are probabilistic, not deterministic. A few things are worth holding onto:

- **Strength does not map cleanly to impact.** The 2015–16 event was very strong; the 1997–98 event was stronger still by some measures but produced a different regional damage pattern. Where the warm anomaly sits in the Pacific matters as much as how warm it gets.
- **Some regions gain.** El Niño years often bring better rainfall to Argentina, parts of the US South, and the Horn of Africa. Global supply can partly self-hedge.
- **Markets adapt.** Farmers switch crops, importers buy forward, and stocks that look thin in a forecast are frequently rebuilt before the forecast horizon arrives.
- **Projected figures are scenario estimates.** The 49 million number is a modeled projection under stated assumptions, not a measurement. It will be revised — plausibly in both directions.

---

## The bottom line

The most useful reframe here is that a climate event and a food crisis are not the same thing separated by time — they are separated by *decisions*. Whether a rainfall anomaly in 2027 becomes a hunger emergency in 2028 depends on seed availability, storage, credit access, trade policy, and whether pre-positioned aid arrives before or after households start selling what they need to recover.

For US shoppers, the practical expectation is modest and uneven: little visible movement in most of the cart, with more noticeable pressure in coffee, chocolate, cooking oils, rice, and sugar — arriving late in 2027 rather than this year, and heavily dependent on trade policy nobody can forecast yet.

For the 225 million people the WFP already counts as food-insecure, the stakes are not measured in percentage points. That asymmetry — a rounding error on one continent, a lean season on another — is the clearest thing this forecast makes visible.

---

*This article is general information, not financial or investment advice. Figures cited reflect projections published by the World Food Programme and are subject to revision; readers should consult WFP, FAO, and NOAA primary sources for current data.*
